topic: 8 handwriting interventions: what works (systematic review)
citation: Hoy MM, Egan MY, Feder KP (2011) A systematic review of interventions to improve handwriting. Can J Occup Ther 78(1):13-25
task_or_setup: Systematic review of randomised and non-randomised controlled trials of interventions an occupational therapist could use to improve written output of school-aged children with handwriting difficulties (searches to January 2010)
comparator: Relaxation/practice with or without EMG; sensory-based training without handwriting practice; handwriting-based practice
key_quantitative_findings: Interventions without handwriting practice, and those with fewer than 20 practice sessions, were ineffective regardless of type; effective occupational therapy must include adequate handwriting practice (abstract).
units_and_conditions: Qualitative synthesis; effect sizes not in the abstract
limitations: Abstract only; children; 11 heterogeneous studies; searches end 2010
relevance_to_design: Sets the bar for any guided-practice mode: it must add to real practice, over many sessions, and be judged on unassisted writing
transferability_reason: Children with handwriting difficulty, the practice population; no device-guided arm
design_implication: Plan practice programmes of >= 20 sessions; measure unassisted writing before and after; the pen cannot replace practice
search_query: PubMed E-utilities esearch/efetch (abstract): Hoy Egan Feder systematic review interventions to improve handwriting

topic: 8 handwriting interventions: kinesthetic training alone (RCT)
citation: Sudsawad P, Trombly CA, Henderson A, Tickle-Degnen L (2002) Testing the effect of kinesthetic training on handwriting performance in first-grade students. Am J Occup Ther 56(1):26-33
task_or_setup: Randomised, blinded three-group trial: kinesthetic training vs handwriting practice vs no treatment; kinesthesis and standardised legibility before and after; teachers' ratings 4 weeks later
participants_or_bench: 45 first-grade children (6-7 y) with kinesthetic deficits and handwriting difficulties
key_quantitative_findings: All groups improved kinesthesis with no group difference; no significant improvement of standardised handwriting legibility in any group; teachers reported improvement in all groups and maintenance at 4 weeks; conclusion: no support for kinesthetic training (abstract).
units_and_conditions: Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA; numbers not in abstract
limitations: Abstract only; short intervention; young children; practice arm also showed no standardised gain
relevance_to_design: Sensing the movement passively (kinesthetic input) did not improve legibility: a caution for guidance that moves the hand
transferability_reason: Kinesthetic training, not device guidance; children
design_implication: Do not claim that feeling the right movement (guidance) improves handwriting without an unassisted retention test

topic: 2 handwriting guidance: robotic guidance helps during practice, not at test
citation: Lüttgen J, Heuer H (2012) The influence of haptic guidance on the production of spatio-temporal patterns. Hum Mov Sci 31(3):519-528
task_or_setup: Practice drawing circles with the velocity profile of ellipses, with robotic guidance vs a control group; test with assistance off
key_quantitative_findings: During practice the guided group was better on shape, timing of the velocity modulation and modulation amplitude; at test (guidance off) the differences largely disappeared, except the amplitude of the velocity modulation, which stayed more accurate after guidance (abstract).
limitations: Abstract only; laboratory pattern, not letters; healthy adults
relevance_to_design: Directly predicts what guided practice with the nose or the board would show: better ink while guided, little carry-over
transferability_reason: Guidance of a drawn spatio-temporal pattern; not handwriting or clinical groups
design_implication: Report guided and unguided (retention) writing separately; fade guidance
search_query: PubMed E-utilities esearch/efetch (abstract): haptic guidance handwriting

topic: 2 handwriting guidance: path guidance vs trajectory (timed) guidance
citation: Basteris A, Bracco L, Sanguineti V (2012) Robot-assisted intermanual transfer of handwriting skills. Hum Mov Sci 31(5):1175-1190
task_or_setup: Planar robot; isolated cursive letters about 5 cm with the non-dominant hand; visual template, path guidance (forces toward the template) or trajectory guidance (toward the timed reference); 3 sessions, retention next day
comparator: Visual guidance; path vs trajectory guidance
key_quantitative_findings: Trajectory-shape improvement was significant only with trajectory guidance (and less with visual guidance); path guidance showed no significant improvement; effects largely retained one day later; movement duration fell in all groups (abstract).
limitations: Abstract only; 5 cm letters on a planar robot; non-dominant hand; healthy adults
relevance_to_design: The nose and board laws in this study are path guidance (nearest template point): the kind that did not improve learning here
transferability_reason: Letter shapes and robot forces, but large letters and intermanual transfer
design_implication: If practice guidance is pursued, test timed (trajectory) guidance against path guidance, with next-day unguided retention

topic: 9 multisensory letter learning: visuo-haptic exploration
citation: Bara F, Gentaz E (2011) Haptics in teaching handwriting: the role of perceptual and visuo-motor skills. Hum Mov Sci 30(4):745-759
task_or_setup: Two training programmes in children: visual-haptic (VH) exploration of letters vs visual (V) exploration; second study of visuo-motor vs perceptual skills as predictors of copying
key_quantitative_findings: VH training improved letter recognition and handwriting quality more than V training; only visuo-motor tasks predicted handwriting copying performance (abstract).
limitations: Abstract only; the child's own finger explores relief letters (active), not device-driven motion
relevance_to_design: Supports multisensory, learner-active letter exploration; says nothing about a pen moving the ink
transferability_reason: Active tactile exploration by children, not guidance of the writing tool
design_implication: Offer letter-shape exploration and tracing tasks in the app; keep the learner the author of the movement

topic: 9 multisensory letter learning: handwriting vs typing for letter recognition
citation: Longcamp M, Zerbato-Poudou MT, Velay JL (2005) The influence of writing practice on letter recognition in preschool children: a comparison between handwriting and typing. Acta Psychol 119(1):67-79
task_or_setup: Three weeks of copying letters either by hand or by typing; two recognition tests one week apart
participants_or_bench: Two groups of 38 children aged 3-5 y
key_quantitative_findings: In the older children, handwriting training gave better letter recognition than typing training (abstract).
limitations: Abstract only; preschool children; effect only in the older subgroup
relevance_to_design: The learner's own letter-forming movements support letter knowledge; a device that forms the letter for the learner may remove that benefit (hypothesis)
transferability_reason: Preschool letter learning; no guidance arm
design_implication: Keep the device's share of the ink motion small in practice modes and test whether guidance changes letter learning

topic: 10 dyslexia: nature of the difficulty and multisensory (Orton-Gillingham) evidence
citation: Peterson RL, Pennington BF (2012) Developmental dyslexia. Lancet 379(9830):1997-2007; with Stevens EA, Austin C, Moore C, Scammacca N, Boucher AN, Vaughn S (2021) Current state of the evidence: examining the effects of Orton-Gillingham reading interventions for students with or at risk for word-level reading disabilities. Except Child 87(4):397-417
task_or_setup: Narrative review of dyslexia; meta-analysis of Orton-Gillingham (direct, explicit, multisensory, structured) reading interventions
participants_or_bench: Reviews (students with or at risk for word-level reading disabilities in the meta-analysis)
key_quantitative_findings: Dyslexia: slow and inaccurate word recognition; the phonological theory remains the most compelling, interacting with other risk factors (Peterson & Pennington). Orton-Gillingham: no statistically significant effect on foundational skills including spelling (ES 0.22, p = 0.40) or on vocabulary and comprehension (ES 0.14, p = 0.59), mean effects positive (Stevens et al.).
units_and_conditions: Effect sizes (standardised mean difference) from the meta-analysis abstract
limitations: Abstracts only; reading outcomes; heterogeneous OG programmes
relevance_to_design: Dyslexia is a language difficulty; moving the pen does not address it; even multisensory teaching lacks strong evidence
transferability_reason: Defines the target condition; intervention evidence is for reading instruction, not devices
design_implication: For dyslexia put the effort in the app: recognise, flag gently, show and read the right spelling, keep a corrected copy; do not market physical guidance as dyslexia treatment

topic: 10 dyslexia: handwriting speed limited by spelling, not by movement
citation: Sumner E, Connelly V, Barnett AL (2014) The influence of spelling ability on handwriting production: children with and without dyslexia. J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn 40(5):1441-1447
task_or_setup: Sentence copying on a digital writing tablet (Eye and Pen); execution speed, pausing, spelling and motor skill as predictors
participants_or_bench: 31 children with dyslexia (mean 9 y 4 m) vs age-matched and spelling-ability-matched (6 y 6 m) children
key_quantitative_findings: Children with dyslexia executed handwriting at the same speed as age-matched peers but wrote less and paused more, especially within words; spelling ability plus within-word pausing explained over 76 % of the variance in their handwriting production; motor skill added no significant variance (abstract).
limitations: Abstract only; children; copying task
relevance_to_design: For dyslexia the pen's movement help targets the wrong bottleneck; spelling support does not
transferability_reason: Dyslexic writers on a tablet; children, not adults
design_implication: Measure pauses and spelling errors (the app can), not only ink quality, for dyslexic users
search_query: PubMed E-utilities esearch/efetch (abstract): Sumner Connelly Barnett dyslexia handwriting pauses

topic: 10 dysgraphia: definitions (spelling vs handwriting) and rehabilitation
citation: McCloskey M, Rapp B (2017) Developmental dysgraphia: an overview and framework for research. Cogn Neuropsychol 34(3-4):65-82; Döhla D, Heim S (2016) Developmental dyslexia and dysgraphia: what can we learn from the one about the other? Front Psychol 6:2045; Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou E, Puyjarinet F, Velay JL, Albaret JM, Chaix Y (2019) Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 15:1873-1885
access_level: abstract (McCloskey & Rapp); full text (Döhla & Heim; Biotteau et al., PMC)
task_or_setup: Reviews of developmental dysgraphia (spelling and handwriting deficits), its relation to dyslexia and DCD, diagnosis and rehabilitation
key_quantitative_findings: 'Developmental dysgraphia' covers both spelling and handwriting deficits, diverse in manifestations and causes (McCloskey & Rapp). Döhla & Heim use it for a writing (spelling) disorder: prevalence of developmental writing disorders about 7-15 % of school-aged children, boys 2-3 times more; phonological awareness matters for both reading and writing. Biotteau et al.: no gold standard for diagnosing handwriting dysgraphia; BHK test = 5-min copy, 13 legibility criteria plus speed, threshold -2 SD; about half of children with DCD have difficulty learning to write; most rehabilitation targets the graphomotor component (models showing the movement, movement-focused attention, tactile/kinesthetic exploration, tablets with supplementary auditory or colour feedback); DCD interventions of at least ~9 weeks tended to be more effective.
locator: Abstract; full texts (definitions, BHK, rehabilitation sections)
limitations: Reviews; terminology differs between countries; few controlled device studies
relevance_to_design: 'Dysgraphia' must be split: motor handwriting difficulty (the pen's feedback and practice modes can help) vs spelling (app AI)
transferability_reason: Definitions and practice evidence for the target users; not device trials
design_implication: State which dysgraphia each function serves; use BHK-like unassisted legibility and speed as the outcome

topic: 10 assistive technology for writing with learning disabilities: spell checkers, smart pens
citation: Perelmutter B, McGregor KK, Gordon KR (2017) Assistive technology interventions for adolescents and adults with learning disabilities: an evidence-based systematic review and meta-analysis. Comput Educ 114:139-163; with MacArthur CA, Graham S, Haynes JB, DeLaPaz S (1996) Spelling checkers and students with learning disabilities: performance comparisons and impact on spelling. J Spec Educ 30(1):35-57
evidence_class: systematic review and meta-analysis; bench comparison + study
task_or_setup: Meta-analysis of AT interventions (word processing/spell checking, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, smart pens, multimedia); MacArthur: 10 spelling checkers on 555 misspellings from 55 students with LD, and their use
participants_or_bench: Adolescents and adults with LD (meta-analysis); students with LD grades 5-8 (MacArthur)

MacArthur et al.: correcting 37 % of errors still leaves 63 % uncorrected (search summary).

topic: PD micrographia: lined paper and grids (pilot)
citation: Bryant MS, Rintala DH, Lai EC, Protas EJ (2010) An investigation of two interventions for micrographia in individuals with Parkinson's disease. Clin Rehabil 24(11):1021-1026
task_or_setup: Single group pre/post: practise writing words with parallel horizontal lines and with grid lines (randomised order); outcome word length
key_quantitative_findings: Word length after practising with parallel lines 23.36 +/- 5.82 cm vs free writing 17.83 +/- 3.93 cm (p = 0.008); after grid lines 22.65 +/- 4.04 cm (p = 0.003); lines vs grid no difference (abstract).
units_and_conditions: Word length in cm (sum over words); immediate
limitations: Abstract only; n = 11 men; immediate effect; no control group
relevance_to_design: Lined paper enlarges PD writing by about 27-31 % immediately: the low-tech comparator for cues and size assist
transferability_reason: PD micrographia, real writing; small pilot
design_implication: Always compare pen functions against lined paper; the app can print or display lines

topic: PD micrographia depends on visual feedback
citation: Ondo WG, Satija P (2007) Withdrawal of visual feedback improves micrographia in Parkinson's disease. Mov Disord 22(14):2130-2131
task_or_setup: Writing 'Today is a nice day' with eyes open and eyes closed (alternated order)
participants_or_bench: 40 PD OFF medication, 40 PD ON, 64 age- and sex-matched controls
key_quantitative_findings: Eye closure increased writing length by 14.0 +/- 10.1 % in OFF PD (69.1 -> 77.7 mm; range -14 % to +73 %); 19.5 % vs 7.9 % in the 20 with the smallest vs larger writing; no change in ON or controls (abstract).
limitations: Abstract only; letter; single session
relevance_to_design: Micrographia is tied to visual feedback: an assist that enlarges the visible ink may interact with the writer's visual control in unknown ways
transferability_reason: PD writing; mechanism evidence, no device
design_implication: Test size assist for adaptation (does the writer's own movement shrink further?) with the hand path logged separately from the ink

topic: How tremor shows in handwriting and spirals: ET vs PD vs dystonic vs functional
citation: Alty J, Cosgrove J, Thorpe D, Kempster P (2017) How to use pen and paper tasks to aid tremor diagnosis in the clinic. Pract Neurol 17(6):456-463
task_or_setup: Clinical review of handwriting, Archimedes spirals and lines for tremor diagnosis
key_quantitative_findings: ET: mostly a unidirectional tremor axis (8-2 o'clock for right-hand spirals), normal size of spirals and handwriting, small amplitude (< 1 cm), regular high frequency (8-12 Hz). PD: slow, small writing, tightly bunched spirals, decrementing size and speed; action tremor in nearly half of patients when drawing. Dystonic tremor: multidirectional, jerky, usually < 7 Hz, hard pen pressure. Functional tremor: inconsistent frequency and axis.
locator: Sections on essential, parkinsonian, dystonic and functional tremor
limitations: Expert review; frequency range quoted for typical cases (older ET patients are often 4-6 Hz, PDT-31)
relevance_to_design: Supports the fixed-axis tremor model and the primer's picture of tremor in ink; PD writing problems are size and speed
transferability_reason: Handwriting and drawing in the target groups
design_implication: Use the pen's recordings to show the tremor axis and frequency; do not treat PD writing as a tremor problem only

topic: PD wrist-finger coordination bias in graphical tasks
citation: Dounskaia N, Van Gemmert AWA, Leis BC, Stelmach GE (2009) Biased wrist and finger coordination in Parkinsonian patients during performance of graphical tasks. Neuropsychologia 47(12):2504-2514
task_or_setup: Circle and line drawing with wrist and finger motions at several speeds
key_quantitative_findings: Both groups deformed circles into right-tilted ovals, significantly more in PD, through reduced relative phase between wrist and fingers rather than amplitude; nonequivalent lines were more variable in PD during fast movements; finger flexion/extension moves the pen up-down, wrist rotation left-right (paper's description).
limitations: Small groups; drawing, not letters
relevance_to_design: PD changes letter shape and slant through joint coordination, beyond size
transferability_reason: PD graphical movements; not handwriting outcomes
design_implication: Include shape and slant measures in PD outcome sets; size assist alone does not address coordination

citation: Dounskaia N, Van Gemmert AWA, Stelmach GE (2000) Interjoint coordination during handwriting-like movements. Exp Brain Res 135(1):127-140

topic: handwriting movement: wrist and finger movement axes are roughly orthogonal
citation: Schomaker LRB, Plamondon R (1990) The relation between pen force and pen-point kinematics in handwriting. Biol Cybern 63:277-289 (as reproduced in Schomaker LRB (1991) PhD thesis, chapter 'Pen force and pen-tip kinematics', Table 1)

key_quantitative_findings: Mean preferred angle to the digitiser x-axis: wrist 39 deg, fingers 134 deg, difference 95 deg (range 79-115 deg over subjects): the wrist and finger systems have approximately orthogonal movement axes; wrist movements were more accurate (narrower patterns) than finger movements.
limitations: Forearm fixed (no arm contribution); young adults; same source as CON-01/02

transferability_reason: Real writers; constrained forearm
design_implication: Tremor at the wrist appears mostly along the wrist axis (about 40 deg); finger tremor along the letter's up-down axis

topic: handwriting movement: oscillation theory (up-down and sideways oscillations on a sweep)
citation: Hollerbach JM (1981) An oscillation theory of handwriting. Biol Cybern 39:139-156
access_level: search-engine summary of the abstract (publisher abstract elided in Semantic Scholar; ACM page 403)
task_or_setup: Model of handwriting as constrained modulation of coupled oscillations
key_quantitative_findings: Coupled horizontal and vertical oscillations produce letter forms; superimposed on a rightward constant-velocity sweep they separate letters; vertical-oscillation modulation controls letter height; horizontal phase/amplitude controls corner shape; the slope at the vertical-velocity zero crossing controls slant.
limitations: Primary text not read; model, not measurement
relevance_to_design: Primer picture: letters = up-down + sideways oscillation (fingers, wrist) + sweep along the line (arm)
transferability_reason: Classic model of cursive writing
design_implication: A size assist acting on the oscillation (strokes) but not on the sweep enlarges letters without moving along the line; it crowds letters unless applied vertically

topic: Guided practice: nose and board guidance vs letter recognition and device authorship (this study)
citation: This ledger's simulation: handwriting/practice.py; results/handwriting/outcomes.json practice
task_or_setup: Writers 0-5 x seeds 200-203 with a dysgraphia-like or dyslexia-like error model; copybook target anchored at touchdown; stroke-matched nose guidance (gain 0.5/1.0, capture gate); guidance board with the board study's law and final parameter file (magnet on the handle, 0.4 N cap, 0.18 mm sensing noise); passive hand
key_quantitative_findings: Dysgraphia-like: ink vs target none 582 um, nose full 225, board full 384; letters read 0.92 / 0.86 / 0.85; device share 38% (nose) and 25% (board). Dyslexia-like: reversed or wrong letters read as the target: none 0.00, nose full 0.00; cue flags 100% of errors
units_and_conditions: Target error = RMS distance of ink to the target letters (um); letters read against the target; device share = device path length / (device + hand)
limitations: Passive hand (no following or resisting); no learning or retention modelled; simple template-matching reader

design_implication: Guidance brings the ink closer to the copybook target during guidance, but the device then authors 20-40 % of the ink motion; full guidance leaves hybrid letters that are read less well, partial nose guidance keeps them readable; no guidance turns a reversed or wrong letter into the right one, so for dyslexia the app's flagging against a known target carries the benefit.
